os-identity.title: Identity
os-identity.summary: The rules of signing in and being allowed: a validated permission catalog and checker, PBKDF2 password hashing with an upgrade path from old hashes, lockout and login throttling, sessions with hashed keys and a security log. With no database package it runs in memory, so a desktop app or a test needs nothing else.

gives.1: Passwords stored with PBKDF2-SHA512 in a text that carries its own cost, so a stronger setting upgrades old rows at the next sign-in.
gives.2: Brute force slowed from two sides: an exponential lock on the account and an in-memory throttle by name and address.
gives.3: A permission catalog that fails at startup on a duplicate or malformed name, and a checker that follows the current principal.

sample.quick: Identity for an app with its own permission tree
sample.signed-in-user: Tell the checker who the current user is

start.title: Getting started
start.summary: One registration gives you the hasher, the lock rules, the catalog, the checker and in-memory sessions.

1.title: One registration
1.text: `AddOSIdentity` registers everything; a second call changes the same options.

2.title: Works without a database
2.text: Sessions and the security log live in memory until the data package replaces them.

3.title: Bad options stop the app
3.text: Policies are validated at registration, not on the first sign-in.

4.title: Startup sync
4.text: `SyncOSIdentityAsync` writes the app and its permissions to the database.

1.title: Registering
1.text:
`AddOSIdentity(o => ...)` takes an `IdentityOptions`: the `App` (an `AppIdentity` with at least a code), the `Session`, `Lock` and `Password` policies, how long a resolved permission set stays fresh (`PermFresh`, 60 seconds), how long the security log is kept (`SecLogRetentionDays`, 365) and an optional `Principal` delegate.

Then add one `IPermProvider` per module with `AddOSPermProvider<T>`. If you do not set the `Principal` delegate, register your own `IPrincipalAccessor` with `AddOSPrincipalAccessor<T>`.

A module can also be registered through `IdentityModule`, whose code is `idn`, so other modules can list it in their `Requires`.

2.title: Options are checked early
2.text:
`IdentityOptions` checks itself when you register: a lock threshold of zero, a negative decay time, an iteration count outside 10,000 to 2,000,000, a maximum password length below the minimum or an app code longer than 24 characters throws at once.

Without this check, a threshold of zero would lock an account on the first typo, and you would find out in production.

3.title: Sync and upkeep
3.text:
`IIdentitySync.SyncAsync` makes the database know your app and its permission tree. Call `SyncOSIdentityAsync` once at startup. `IIdentityMaintenance.PurgeAsync` removes old sessions and old security log rows; run it from a background job.

Both have no implementation in this package, because both need a database. The data package provides them. Calling the sync without it fails with a clear error.

register.title: Register with your own policies
register.note: Idle time of eight hours and a lock after three misses; the permission tree comes from `ShopPerms`.

own-principal-source.title: Say who the current user is
own-principal-source.note: A delegate that returns the principal of the current request or window.

sync-at-startup.title: Sync once at startup
sync-at-startup.note: Needs the data package; it writes the app row and the permission tree.

check-apermission.title: Check a permission
check-apermission.note: `Require` returns nothing when allowed and a Forbidden result otherwise.

bad-options.title: A bad option stops the registration
bad-options.note: The error names the option, so the fix is obvious.

type.IdentityOptions: The app, the policies, the cache time and the log retention.
type.IIdentitySync: Writes the app row and the permission tree to the database.
type.IIdentityMaintenance: Removes old sessions and old security log rows.

IdentityEx.AddOSIdentity: Registers the identity services and validates the options at once. A second call changes the same options and registers nothing twice.
IdentityEx.AddOSPermProvider: Adds a permission provider; each module adds its own.
IdentityEx.AddOSLoginSource: Registers your `ILoginSource`, the one class an app writes to let the library find users.
IdentityEx.AddOSLoginMethod: Adds one more way to sign in; the password method is always there.

passwords.title: Passwords
passwords.summary: Hash, verify and upgrade passwords. The stored text says how it was made, so old rows keep working.

1.title: PBKDF2-SHA512
1.text: A random 32-byte salt, 220,000 iterations by default, a 64-byte hash.

2.title: Upgrades itself
2.text: A hash with a lower cost or an old algorithm is rewritten at the next good sign-in.

3.title: Bad input is false, not a crash
3.text: A damaged hash text or a huge password makes `Verify` return false.

4.title: No timing leak for unknown users
4.text: `Burn` spends the same time as a real check.

1.title: Hash and verify
1.text:
`IPasswordHasher.Hash` makes a text like `pbkdf2-sha512$220000$salt$hash`: the algorithm, the iteration count, the salt and the hash, the last two in base64. `Verify(password, stored)` recomputes with the stored salt and cost and compares in constant time.

It returns false, never throws, for a null or empty password, a password over 1,024 bytes, and a stored text that is damaged: wrong number of parts, zero or negative iterations, an iteration count above two million, bad base64 or a hash of the wrong length. A damaged row therefore means a refused sign-in, not a server error and not a CPU bomb.

2.title: Upgrading old hashes
2.text:
`NeedsRehash(stored)` is true when the text is damaged, when it uses the old `hmac-sha512` algorithm, or when its iteration count is lower than the policy. After a successful `Verify`, call `Hash` again and save the new text; `LockGuard.Check` does this for you.

`FromLegacy(salt, hash)` wraps an old salted HMAC-SHA512 value in the same text format, so you can import those rows without asking anyone for a new password. The old algorithm is accepted only for verifying and is always rewritten after a good sign-in.

3.title: Policy and temporary passwords
3.text:
`PasswordPolicy` has `Iterations` (default 220,000, allowed 10,000 to 2,000,000), `MinLength` (8), `MaxLength` (128) and `TempHours` (72). The length rules apply when a user sets a password through `LockGuard.SetSecret`.

`NewTemp` makes a random temporary password with the cryptographic generator. The alphabet leaves out look-alike letters such as `l`, `I`, `O`, `0` and `1`, so it can be read over the phone. No Unicode normalization is applied to passwords: it would invalidate every stored hash.

The class `PasswordHash` is the parsed form of the stored text; you rarely need it directly.

hash-and-verify.title: Hash and verify
hash-and-verify.note: The algorithm name leads the stored text. The right password passes and a wrong one does not.

stored-text.title: What the stored text holds
stored-text.note: Four parts: algorithm, cost, salt and hash.

upgrade.title: A lower cost asks for a rehash
upgrade.note: A hash made with 50,000 iterations is old for a 220,000 policy; a new hash is not.

legacy-hash.title: Import an old HMAC hash
legacy-hash.note: It verifies, and it always asks to be rewritten.

damaged.title: Damaged text is just false
damaged.note: No exception, so a broken row cannot crash the sign-in.

temporary-password.title: A readable temporary password
temporary-password.note: Ten characters, none of them easy to mistake.

type.PasswordHasher: PBKDF2-SHA512 with a random salt and a cost from the policy.

lockout.title: Lockout and throttling
lockout.summary: Slow a guessing attack from two sides: lock the account after repeated misses, and slow the name and address that keep missing.

1.title: Lock grows each time
1.text: Five minutes at the fifth miss, ten at the sixth, up to an hour.

2.title: Old misses are forgiven
2.text: After 30 quiet minutes the counter starts again.

3.title: A throttle in front
3.text: `LoginThrottle` counts by name and by address in memory, so parallel requests cannot hide.

4.title: Time is injected
4.text: Everything uses `TimeProvider`, so the rules are tested with a fake clock.

1.title: The account lock
1.text:
`LockGuard` works on any `ILockable`. `RegisterFailure` adds one miss and returns the lock time. Below the threshold (5 by default) there is no lock. From the threshold on, the lock is `BaseLockMinutes` (5) doubled for each extra miss, up to `MaxLockMinutes` (60). A miss older than `DecayMinutes` (30), counted from the last miss or the end of the last lock, starts the count again.

`IsLocked`, `Remaining` and `Clear` read and reset the three lock fields. `Backoff.Delay(failures, free, first, max)` is the one formula both the account lock and the throttle use.

2.title: Checking a login
2.text:
`Check(login, account, password)` runs the whole decision in order: locked, wrong password (which counts a miss), account or login disabled, temporary password expired. On success it clears the misses, rewrites an old hash and returns `Ok` with `NeedsSave`, which means you must save the row. A wrong password also returns `NeedsSave`, because the miss count changed.

When no user is found, return `CheckMissing()`: it burns the time of one hash so a missing name costs the same as a wrong password.

`SetSecret` checks the password length policy and returns a result with a field error when it does not fit. `SetTempSecret` stores a temporary password with an expiry; `IsTempSecretExpired` tells when it ended.

3.title: The throttle
3.text:
The lock lives in the user row, and parallel requests can read the same miss count before any of them saves. `LoginThrottle` closes that gap: it keeps a count per lower-cased name and per address in memory. From the fifth miss it asks the caller to wait 30 seconds, doubling up to 15 minutes. Ask `RetryAfter(name, address)` before you check a password; call `Failed` on a miss. `Succeeded(name)` clears the name only, so a person who signs in to their own account cannot wipe the count of an address that keeps failing. A count also fades after a long quiet time.

It is bounded: it holds at most 10,000 entries and drops the oldest when full. It lives in one process, so behind several servers keep a rate limiter in front too.

lock-after-five.title: The lock grows with each miss
lock-after-five.note: Nothing for four misses, then 5, 10 and 20 minutes.

check-alogin.title: Check a login
check-alogin.note: A wrong password counts a miss; the right one clears it and asks you to save.

lock-expires.title: A lock ends by itself
lock-expires.note: The clock is a fake one, so the sample moves time forward.

backoff-table.title: The shared formula
backoff-table.note: Failures below five cost nothing; then the wait doubles up to the maximum.

throttle.title: Slow a name and an address
throttle.note: The name is slowed from any address, and the address from any name, but an unrelated pair is free.

unknown-user.title: A name that does not exist
unknown-user.note: It looks like any wrong password, and costs the same time.

type.LockGuard: Lock rules, the full login check and the secret setters, on any `ILogin`.
type.LockPolicy: Threshold, decay time, first lock and maximum lock.
type.LoginThrottle: An in-memory slow-down by name and by address; bounded and thread safe.
type.Backoff: The doubling wait used by the lock and the throttle.

LockGuard.Check: Locked, wrong password, disabled, temporary password expired, or success; `NeedsSave` says the row changed and must be saved.
LockGuard.CheckMissing: Use it when the user was not found: same cost, same answer as a wrong password.

perms.title: The permission catalog and checker
perms.summary: Collect every module's tree, check it once, expand wildcards, and answer "may this user do that?".

1.title: Fails at startup
1.text: A duplicate name, a malformed name or a foreign app prefix throws when the catalog is built.

2.title: Wildcards expand once
2.text: `shop:orders:*` becomes a fixed list of names, cached per pattern.

3.title: Cache with a short life
3.text: A resolved set stays fresh for 60 seconds; an edit can clear it at once on this server.

1.title: The catalog
1.text:
`PermCatalog` is built from every registered `IPermProvider`. Names must be lower case segments joined by `:` (letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`), at most 128 characters, with the app code as the first segment. A name declared twice is an error, and so is a tree deeper than 32 levels. The error is an `OSException` at startup, not a surprise on the first request.

`Find(name)`, `ForApp(code)`, `Flat`, `Roots` and `Names` read it. `Expand(pattern)` returns the names a pattern covers; a plain name returns itself, even when it is not in the catalog. `IsLive` tells whether a pattern matches anything now, which is how an editor finds orphan patterns. `Uncovered(checker, patterns)` lists the known names the current user does not hold; it is the basis of the ceiling rule that stops people granting more than they have.

2.title: Patterns and the checker
2.text:
`PermPattern` owns the wildcard syntax in one place: `*` covers everything, `a:b:*` covers every name that starts with `a:b:`, and any other text covers only itself. `Covers`, `IsWildcard`, `IsValidName` and `Normalize` are public so your own screens use the same rules.

`PermChecker` reads the current user from the `IPrincipalAccessor` on every call. No user means no permission. Names are lower-cased before the check. `IsGranted(name, chain)` follows a scope chain, with the nearest scope winning.

`PermGrantBuilder` turns the catalog into the trees an editor shows: `ToRoleGrants` for a role with its patterns, and `ToGrant` for a user with the role access and the overrides.

3.title: Resolving and caching
3.text:
`IPermResolver.ResolveAsync(userId)` builds a user's `PermSet`; the data package provides it. `IPermCache` sits in front: `GetAsync` returns the set from `HybridCache` for `PermFresh` (60 seconds) and `InvalidateAsync` clears one user. Without `HybridCache` registered it passes straight through. Register `AddOSCaching` to turn it on.

On several servers a clear reaches only the current server; the others keep the old set until it expires, so a revoked permission can live for up to 60 seconds there.

Three accessors are ready: `DelegatePrincipalAccessor` wraps a function, `AmbientPrincipalAccessor` keeps the principal per async flow with `Set`, and you can register your own class.

catalog.title: Read the catalog
catalog.note: Five names, the parent of a child, and the names a wildcard covers.

wildcard-rules.title: The wildcard rules
wildcard-rules.note: A trailing `:*` covers a branch, a plain name covers itself, and a name with a space is not valid.

duplicate-name.title: A duplicate stops startup
duplicate-name.note: Two providers declare the same names.

scoped-deny.note: Allowed everywhere, denied in store 5, so store 6 still allows it.

role-tree.title: The tree an editor shows
role-tree.note: A role that holds `shop:orders:*` has access to the group and to each child.

what-the-caller-lacks.title: The ceiling rule
what-the-caller-lacks.note: What a caller cannot hand out, because they do not hold it themselves.

sessions.title: Sessions and the security log
sessions.summary: Open a session with a secret key that is stored only as a hash, touch it, revoke it, and record what happened.

1.title: Only a hash is stored
1.text: The key is 32 random bytes; a stolen table cannot be used to sign in.

2.title: Three ways to end
2.text: A session can be revoked, expire after 30 days, or go idle after 4 hours.

3.title: Touch is throttled
3.text: `LastSeenDate` is written at most once a minute per session.

4.title: The log never blocks sign-in
4.text: A failed log write returns false; it does not throw into the login.

1.title: The store
1.text:
`ISessionStore` has eight calls. `CheckAsync(id)` reads the state of a session without its key, for a signed token that already proves who holds it. `OpenAsync(userId, client)` returns an `OpenedSession`: the id, the key and the expiry; the client texts are clamped first. `TouchAsync(id, key)` checks the key against the hash in constant time and returns a `SessionState`. `ListAsync` returns a user's sessions for a screen. `RevokeAsync` and `RevokeUserAsync` end one session or all of a user's, optionally keeping the current one, and record the reason and who did it. `IsFreshClientAsync` tells whether this device has never signed in before. `PurgeAsync` removes sessions long past their end.

`MemorySessionStore` is the default: it keeps sessions in memory, which is right for one desktop app or for tests. The data package replaces it with a database store.

2.title: Keys and rules
2.text:
`SessionKeys.New` makes the random key, `Hash` makes the SHA-256 text that is stored and `Matches` compares them without leaking time. `SessionRules.Check` decides the state from the dates and the policy: revoked first, then expired, then idle. `ShouldTouch` says whether the last-seen date is old enough to write again.

`SessionPolicy` has `AbsoluteDays` (30), `IdleHours` (4), `RetentionDays` (30) and `TouchSeconds` (60). A web app that wants shorter sessions sets its own values; the defaults are not tied to any app type.

3.title: The security log
3.text:
`ISecLog.WriteAsync(entry)` records a `SecLogEntry` and returns whether it was written. It fills the app code and the date when they are empty, clamps every text and masks a suspicious target.

`MemorySecLog` keeps the last 1,000 entries in memory and shows them in `Recent`. With the data package the log goes to a table through its own database context, so writing a log line never saves anything else you had pending, and a failure is reported to the error sink instead of being swallowed.

open-and-touch.title: Open and touch a session
open-and-touch.note: The key is shown once; only the right key is valid.

idle.title: An idle session
idle.note: Five hours without a touch is past the four-hour limit.

revoke.title: Revoke with a reason and a person
revoke.note: The reason is a code and the actor is a user id.

long-user-agent.title: A long client name
long-user-agent.note: Cut to 128 characters before it is stored.

security-log.title: Two log lines
security-log.note: A name is kept; text that looks like a password is replaced by a short hash.

login.title: Signing in
login.summary: One service runs a sign-in: the throttle, the chosen method, the lock, the session and the log. A method decides what proves who you are.

1.title: Not only passwords
1.text: A password, a code sent to a phone or mail, a safe link, a passkey and a second factor are all methods behind one interface.

2.title: You write one class
2.text: `ILoginSource` finds users in your table and saves the lock fields; the library does the rest.

3.title: A step can be asked for
3.text: A method can answer with a challenge, and the answer finishes the sign-in later.

4.title: Everything is logged
4.text: Each try, lock, challenge and session leaves a security log line.

1.title: The flow
1.text:
`StartAsync(request)` does this in order: refuses an empty or very long name; asks `LoginThrottle` whether this name or address must wait (the answer is `Throttled` with the wait time, and nothing is verified); finds the method named in the request, or the password method; asks the method; saves the user row when the method says it changed; then acts on the answer.

On success it clears the throttle for the name, opens a session and logs `LoginTried` and `SessionOpened`. On a failure it counts the miss for the name and the address, logs it with a short reason code, and returns the state: `InvalidCred`, `Locked` (with the time left), `Disabled`, `TempPassExpired` or `Throttled`. A name that does not exist counts and fails exactly like a wrong password, so the answer never says which part was wrong.

`LoginOutcome` carries the state, the opened session (with its one-time key), the subject, the lock time, the retry time and, for a challenge, its id and kind.

2.title: Your user table: ILoginSource
2.text:
`ILoginSource` has three calls: `FindAsync(identifier)` (a name, an email or a mobile number, your choice), `FindByIdAsync(id)` and `SaveAsync(subject)`. They return and save a `LoginSubject`: the user id, the user name, the full name, the `ILogin` and `IAccount` of the user, and a `State` object of your own that you get back unchanged.

The library never sees your table. It changes the lock fields through the interfaces and tells you when to save.

3.title: Ways to sign in: ILoginMethod
3.text:
A method has a `Provider` name (`password`, or `code`, `magic-link`, `passkey` and so on) and one call, `VerifyAsync(request, source)`. It answers with a `MethodResult`: `Signed(subject)`, `Failed(state, reason)` or `Challenge(subject, kind, answer)`.

`PasswordMethod` is built in. It finds the user, burns the time of a hash when there is none, and runs the lock rules of `LockGuard`. Add your own with `AddOSLoginMethod<T>()`; the request chooses it by name. The library does not send codes or mails; your method does, and hands the expected answer to the library, which stores only a hash of it.

4.title: Challenges
4.text:
When a method answers `Challenge`, `StartAsync` stores the expected answer, hashed with a random salt, and returns a `ChallengeId`. `ContinueAsync(id, answer, client)` finishes the sign-in later with the answer the user typed or the token from a link. The usual cases are a code to a phone, a safe link in a mail, or a second factor after a password.

A challenge lives 10 minutes, allows 5 tries, and can be used once. A wrong answer says how many tries are left; a used, expired or unknown challenge simply fails. `ILoginChallenges` is the store; `MemoryLoginChallenges` keeps them in this process, so behind several servers register a shared implementation. The account is checked again at the end, so a user disabled in the meantime cannot finish.

5.title: Signing out
5.text: `LogoutAsync(sessionId, userId)` ends one session and logs `SessionClosed`. `LogoutAllAsync(userId, keep)` ends all the user's sessions, optionally keeping the current one, and logs `SessionRevoked`. Both give the actor and the reason to the session store.

own-method.title: Write your own method
own-method.note: A code by mail: it sends the code and gives the expected answer to the library.

register.title: Register the source and a method
register.note: The password method is already there.

sign-in.title: A wrong and a right password
sign-in.note: Both are logged; the right one returns a session with its key.

throttled.title: A name that does not exist
throttled.note: Five misses slow the name and the address, and the real name from the same address waits too.

second-factor.title: A code as a second step
second-factor.note: The first call asks for a challenge; a wrong code costs a try, the right one signs in, and it works once.

logout.title: Sign out
logout.note: One session first, then all the others.
